newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Tsarist debt suspended on eve of Paris talks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Tsarist debt suspended on eve of Paris talks.

text.p: The French stock market suspended trading in Tsarist-era Russian debt on Monday on the eve of talks in Paris with Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on compensation for French bond holders, officials said.

Russia returned to the international capital markets last Thursday with a $1.0 billion five-year Eurobond, but it was not placed in France because of outstanding compensation claims by holders of debt issued before the 1917 Communist revolution.
Chernomyrdin, who is running the Kremlin while President Boris Yeltsin recovers from heart surgery, was due in Paris on Monday night for two days of talks on closer economic relations.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis and Foreign Minister Herve de Charette were to meet representatives of French bond holders on Monday to discuss the French negotiating position, prompting French press speculation of a possible deal.
But French officials said the negotiation was complex and they doubted a deal could be struck during Chernomyrdin's visit.
In Moscow, the Russian Finance Ministry said Deputy Finance Minister Mikhail Kasyanov, a senior expert on foreign debt, would accompany Chernomyrdin to discuss the Tsarist bonds issue.

"Because of rumours relayed by various information services relative to Russian loans, the listing of these is provisionally suspended from today, November 25, 1996," the Paris stock market said in an announcement.

French Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said last Friday that Paris hoped long-running talks with Moscow on compensation could be concluded soon so that new bonds issued by the post-Communist authorities could be subscribed in France.
"There have been negotiations for many years. We hope that they will finally be completed so that French savers can again respond to the financing needs of the Russian state," he said.
Russia defaulted on its loans, used to finance big projects such as the Transsiberian railroad, after the Communists seized power in 1917.

French investors were heavy buyers of the bonds, issued between 1822 and 1913, and thousands of small savers were left holding virtually worthless certificates that can be bought as framed curiosities in antique shops.
The successors of the original buyers are claiming back some 140 to 160 billion francs ($27.5-$31 billion), taking account of unpaid interest since the Soviet revolution.
However officials said Moscow argues that any liability for Tsarist era debt must be offset against the seizure of Russian assets in the West after 1917 which were used to help fight the communists.
On October 29, Russian newsagency Itar-Tass quoted Finance Minister Alexandre Livshits as saying that French and Russian negotiators were close to agreement on a "symbolic" gesture.

Accompanied by his ministers of agriculture, energy and communications and the head of the Russian space agency, Chernomyrdin will hold talks with President Jacques Chirac, Prime Minister Alain Juppe and Foreign Minister Herve de Charette on economic cooperation and international issues.
He is due to hold a joint news conference with Juppe on Tuesday afternoon.
